name: Face reveal threads

lead: A face reveal thread is a forum post where a member, who has usually posted anonymously or with a masked photo, shares an unobscured picture of their face. The community then rates it and, often, recommends where to focus: skin, hair, body fat, facial hair, glasses, or procedures.

The appearance payoff is feedback: members say it gives them a reference point and a prioritized to-do list. Ratings use the community's own scales and terms such as 'chadlite' or 'high-tier normie', which are subjective and vary from rater to rater. No research has evaluated forum ratings as a guide to improvement.

paras: Members typically post front and side photos in neutral lighting along with basic stats, and ask for ratings or advice. Raters reply with a tier, a list of perceived strengths and weaknesses, and suggestions. Some members post a 'reveal' after a transformation to show progress.

A posted photo can be copied, reposted or traced to the person, and some threads attract harsh or mocking replies. Ratings reflect individual opinion. Members who are concerned about privacy sometimes send photos privately to a single rater instead.

web.title: What does PSL mean? - Know Your Meme

chain: Choose what to improve (skin, hair, weight, grooming)
angle.text: The thread itself does not change a face. Members use the comments as a map of which changes to pursue, such as grooming, skin or body-fat changes, and later post updates to show the outcome.

lead: A face reveal thread is a post on a looksmaxxing forum in which a member shows their unmasked face to the community for rating and advice. Members who have posted anonymously or behind a cropped or masked photo share clear front and side photographs, often with height, age and other stats, and ask what the community sees and what to work on. The practice is common on looksmax.org, where titles such as 'face reveal', 'rate me' and 'face reveal after 4 years' recur [1][2][3].

The payoff members describe is an outside reference point. Replies commonly assign a tier on community scales and list features seen as strong or weak, which members then turn into a to-do list covering skin, hair, body fat, facial hair, glasses, grooming or procedures. Some posters report a private rating, for example saying a rater placed them in a given tier [1]. Others post a reveal after a transformation to document progress, as in a thread titled 'face reveal after 4 years' [2].

The ratings use vocabulary from the PSL scale, a numbered attractiveness scale that Know Your Meme and Wikipedia say originated on the now-defunct PUAHate, SlutHate and Lookism forums, whose initials give the scale its name [4][5][6]. Critics, including researchers Anda Iulia Solea and Lisa Sugiura quoted by Know Your Meme, call the scale pseudoscientific [4]. No published study has examined forum face ratings as a guide to improvement; research on facial attractiveness ratings in general exists but was not designed around this practice.

paras: Face reveal posts follow a loose template: photos from the front and side in neutral lighting, sometimes with height and age, and a request for a rating or an improvement plan. Titles run from a plain 'face reveal' to 'rate me and my stats' [1][7][8]. Some members use the phrase for the first time they show their face after long anonymity [2][7], and others announce an upcoming reveal in advance, as in a thread titled 'prepare for my face reveal' [9].

Responses usually have three parts: a tier or numeric score, a list of perceived strengths and weaknesses, and suggestions. Raters in the community sometimes give a score on the PSL scale, which Know Your Meme describes as running from about 0 to 8 and divided into categories from 'subhuman' through 'normie', 'Chadlite', 'Chad' and 'Adam' [4]. Its mid-range 'normie' labels are often abbreviated LTN, MTN and HTN for low-, mid- and high-tier normie [6]. The category boundaries are described differently by different sources and by different members, and the scale is a community convention rather than a fixed standard [4][5][6].

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says the term and the practice of rating faces originated on message boards of the 2010s, including PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net, collectively called the PSL forums, and that rating men's faces on a numbered scale was a core activity there [5]. Know Your Meme says forum users built the PSL scale in the mid-to-late 2010s and that looksmaxxing communities revived it in the 2020s, when people began casually calling others 'high PSL' or 'low PSL' [6].

Wikipedia records that looksmaxxing spread on TikTok in the early 2020s and received mainstream coverage from Business Insider and The New York Times in November 2023, followed by The Conversation, The Guardian and the BBC in early 2024 [5]. Livestreamer Braden Peters, known as Clavicular, is named by Wikipedia and Know Your Meme among the figures who helped spread rating terms to wider audiences, with news coverage of him in February 2026 [4][5][6]. Individual reveals by well-known online personalities have also become discussion topics on the forums: one looksmax.org thread presents a popular YouTuber's reveal as an example for the blackpill, a worldview in which looks are seen as largely fixed and decisive [10]. 'Face reveal' is also a general internet term for creators who show their face for the first time, as in a 2026 Hacker News post about a YouTube channel [11].

Posters commonly share several angles, often with stats such as height and age, and say what they want feedback on: overall tier, a single feature, or a plan. Raters reply in the thread, and the poster may update with later photos. Some members send photos privately to a single trusted rater rather than posting publicly and then report the verdict in a thread [1]. Another common format is the before-and-after reveal, in which a member shows a transformation after months or years of work [2].

Reveal threads are one of the forum's main social rituals. They give members a shared scale and a record of change, and the replies show the community's standards: terms such as 'chadlite' and 'high-tier normie' appear in ratings, and ratings are sometimes celebrated or contested in the replies [1][4].

Members also use reveals as evidence in broader arguments, for example about whether looks are fixed [10]. Looksmax.org threads also include debates about the rating scale itself; Know Your Meme and Wikipedia both report criticism that beauty cannot be reduced to geometry and that celebrities with traits the scale marks as flaws are nonetheless widely seen as attractive [4][5][6].

Because a reveal photo identifies the poster, members and commentators point to risks such as copying, reposting and tracing the person to their real identity, and some threads attract mocking replies. Wikipedia reports that on some incel forums, users judged below average have been harassed, and cites BBC coverage in 2024 linking appearance-rating communities to body dysmorphia concerns [5]. Ratings come from individuals with differing tastes and no clinical training; they are opinions, not assessments by dermatologists or surgeons.
No studies found. Research on how people rate facial attractiveness in general exists, but no published study has evaluated forum face reveals or community tier ratings.

lore.intro: Reveals and rate-me posts are a staple of looksmax.org, used both to get feedback and to display progress [1][2]. Members and critics disagree about how much the resulting ratings mean.

claims.claim: Community ratings give an accurate read of where a face stands and what to fix
The PSL scale measures attractiveness objectively through facial geometry
A private rating from a trusted rater is more useful than a public thread
A before-and-after reveal shows what looksmaxxing can achieve
A famous person's reveal illustrates the blackpill idea that looks are fixed
Posting an unmasked photo can expose the poster to harassment

timeline.event: PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism forums host face rating on numbered scales; the PSL name is formed from the three [4][5].
Forum users build the PSL scale to rate faces by geometry and symmetry, per Know Your Meme [6].
Looksmaxxing content spreads on TikTok, framed by many as self-improvement [5].
Business Insider and The New York Times cover looksmaxxing [5].
The Conversation, The Guardian and the BBC publish coverage, including mental-health concerns [5].
News coverage of livestreamer Clavicular and the PSL scale; Know Your Meme adds a PSL entry [4][5].
